doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Growing up on guitar, Brubeck, Monk and big bands at home
summary: Gates calls jazz life an adventure, turned pro at 39, and recalls his father's records and early Brubeck and Monk albums.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And because of the hour, I’ll start with a really easy question. This is a fill in the blank. Life as a jazz artist is —

An adventure. And interesting. But I wouldn’t have it any other way. I did a lot of other things before I did this. I started to do this on a professional level at 39 years old, which is about three or four years ago.

And yeah, it’s an interesting ride. The whole thing that got me into this, along with the music, because I’m not old enough to have been there when it was really happening. I might have been on the planet in the 1950s, but I wasn’t making any clubs. But I was a fan of this music, I still am a fan of the music. I got lucky and took some guitar lessons as a very young kid and my instructors were jazz aficionados, jazz players. So my father played classical music around the house. He also played violin, not as a professional musician, but he played violin. He played pretty good. So I was exposed to classical music, but he also played big bands. He played Basie and Cab Calloway and Ellington and Fletcher Henderson. So I got to hear it. And at a very young age I got turned on to Dave Brubeck, about 1950— I don’t know — 7, 8.

Yeah, early Brubeck. I was probably ten. And I listened to Brubeck and I was taking guitar lessons, and I think I bought — I didn’t buy it, my parents bought it for me because I wanted it — the “Time Out” album. And I had no idea what they were doing time-wise. I couldn’t — it was brand new to me. And then the next album I got ahold of was Thelonious Monk. So he played in four. But that was a whole ‘nother thing too. So that’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
kind of where it started and I got hip to Dexter Gordon, Charlie Parker, Lambert, Hendricks & Ross and Joe Williams and on and on and on.
